title: Best Hand from Both Ends
statement:
A row of cards lies on the table. Card i is worth points[i]. You take exactly k cards, one at a time, and each time you must take either the leftmost or the rightmost card still on the table.

Return the largest total you can collect.

examples.why: Take the three cards on the right: 4 + 2 + 9. Always grabbing the bigger end gives 5, then 4, then 2 = 11, because the greedy pick never looks past the next card.
k is the whole row, so every card is taken.
Both from the left. The 100 is reachable only by first taking the 1 in front of it.

hints: The order you take cards in does not matter, only which cards end up taken. What shapes can the set of taken cards have?
You always take some number i of cards from the left and k − i from the right. There are only k + 1 such splits.
Equivalently, the cards you leave are one contiguous block of length n − k. Slide a window of that length and minimise its sum, or move one card at a time from the left part to the right part.

explain.intuition:
The order of picks hides a simple shape. However you interleave left and right picks, you end up with a prefix of length i and a suffix of length k − i. So there are only k + 1 possible hands, and the greedy "take the bigger end" idea fails because it never looks past the next card.

Flip the view: the cards you leave form one contiguous block of length n − k. Maximising what you take is minimising that block. A fixed-size sliding window finds the cheapest block in one pass. Another way to see it: start with all k cards from the left, then move them to the right one at a time, adjusting the sum by one card out and one card in.
steps: Let total be the sum of all cards and w = n − k the size of the block left behind.
Sum the first w cards as the current window.
Slide the window one step at a time: add the card entering on the right, subtract the one leaving on the left, and track the minimum.
Return total − minimum. If w = 0, that is simply total.
pitfalls: Greedily taking the larger end each turn. The first example shows a bigger reward hiding behind a smaller card.
Recomputing every split's sum from scratch, which is O(k²) and too slow for large k.
Mishandling k = n: the window of left-behind cards is empty, and the answer is the sum of everything.

solutions.title: Try every split, summing each
solutions.idea: For each i from 0 to k, add the first i cards and the last k − i cards from scratch.

solutions.title: Shift cards from the left end to the right end
solutions.idea: Start with the first k cards. Then k times, give back the innermost left card and take the next card from the right, keeping the best sum.

solutions.title: Cheapest block left behind
solutions.idea: The untaken cards are one contiguous block of n − k cards. Slide a window of that size, find the smallest sum, and subtract it from the total.

followups: Each card also has a cost, and you can spend at most B. Does the window idea still work?
You may take from either end, but at most m cards from each side. How do you restrict the splits?
